chung.Syllabus Name: Natural Language Processing_Xử lý ngôn ngữ tự nhiên
chung.Learning-Teaching Method: In-class lecture, guided discussion, seminar/presentation, project supervision, peer review, Social Constructivism, Active Learning, Project-based learning, Research-based learning and teaching
chung.Time Allocation: Study hour (150h) = 45h (60 sessions) contact hours + 1h final exam + 104h self-study
chung.Description: This course provides students with a foundation in core concepts and methods of Natural Language Processing. The course covers text classification, vector space models, probabilistic methods, sequence models, attention, and transformer-based approaches. Through a research-oriented team project, students learn how to define an NLP problem, review related work, select datasets, build baseline and improved models, evaluate results, analyze errors, and report findings clearly. By the end of the course, students are expected to understand major NLP techniques, apply them to real problems, design and compare experiments, and write technical reports and a short research paper.
chung.StudentTasks:
- Complete assigned Coursera specialization modules, videos, and slide readings before each week.

- Attend at least 80% of contact sessions (equivalent scheduled class time) in order to be accepted to the final examination.

- Work in a project team to formulate an NLP research problem, collect or select data, and maintain a reproducible repository.

- Submit Progress Set evidence and 4 milestone reports on time: proposal/literature review, baseline method, advanced-model progress, and final paper/presentation.

- Read selected papers or technical notes related to the project topic, cite sources properly, and participate in peer review and revision.

clo: Explain the end-to-end NLP pipeline, text preprocessing, corpus preparation, tokenization, and core linguistic concepts used in natural language processing.
Apply classical NLP methods including vectorization, Naive Bayes, edit-distance reasoning, HMM/POS tagging, n-gram language modeling, and word embeddings to baseline NLP tasks.
Build and analyze neural sequence models for NLP, including feed-forward networks for text, RNN/LSTM/GRU models, and attention-based sequence learning ideas.
Use transformer-based pretrained language models for classification, sequence labeling, retrieval, question answering, and generation-oriented workflows.
Evaluate NLP systems with suitable metrics, perform error analysis, discuss bias and limitations, and justify research conclusions with evidence and reproducible experiments.

Implement an end-to-end NLP research project including problem formulation, data collection or selection, baseline development, improved modeling, evaluation, report writing, short paper writing, and presentation.
Use AI-assisted development tools responsibly to accelerate experimentation, documentation, teamwork, and reflective learning in NLP projects.

cauHoiKienTao: How should an NLP project be scoped so that the problem, dataset, metric, and expected contribution are all feasible within a 10-week course?
When is logistic regression a stronger baseline than a more complex model for sentiment analysis, and what evidence would justify that choice?
Which assumptions of Naive Bayes fail in real text data, and why can the model still remain competitive as a research baseline?
How do representation choices change the geometry of a vector space model and the quality of translation or retrieval decisions built on top of it?
Where does minimum edit distance fail to capture realistic language behavior, and what additional evidence should an autocorrect system use?
What makes a project proposal and literature review convincing enough to show novelty, feasibility, and clear evaluation criteria?
Why can globally optimized decoding outperform local decisions in sequence labeling, and how would you demonstrate that experimentally?
How can we tell whether an n-gram language model is genuinely informative rather than simply memorizing frequent patterns?
What evidence shows that dense word embeddings add value beyond sparse features for a particular task, and how should bias in embedding spaces be examined?
What makes an experimental design reproducible and fair when comparing multiple NLP baselines on the same dataset?
When does a neural sentiment model genuinely outperform a classical baseline, and what evidence is needed beyond a single accuracy gain?
Which linguistic dependencies justify moving from classical language models to RNN/GRU-style sequence models, and how would you show that empirically?
How do gradient problems, memory design, and annotation quality together influence LSTM/NER performance on sequence-labeling tasks?
When is a Siamese architecture preferable to a cross-encoder or other alternatives for semantic similarity tasks?
What counts as meaningful progress in an NLP research project: higher metrics alone, or also stronger analysis, error diagnosis, and reproducibility?
What does attention capture that recurrent encoder-decoder models often miss, and what evidence can support claims about its usefulness?
How do self-attention and transformer design choices alter accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability relative to recurrent models?
Why can transfer-learning models produce fluent but unsupported answers, and how do long-context limits change how we should evaluate QA systems?
What separates a strong final NLP paper from a weak one in terms of claim quality, evidence, structure, citations, and limitations?
After completing the project, what conclusions can be drawn about task-model fit, reproducibility, error analysis, and the limits of current NLP methods?
